##  {#problem data-menu-title="The Problem"}

[The Messy Spreadsheet Problem]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Scenario:** You inherit a dataset

Looks fine in Excel...

But when you try to analyze it:
- R can't understand it
- Plotting fails mysteriously  
- Group calculations give wrong answers

**Why?** The data isn't **tidy**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#tidy-matters data-menu-title="Why Tidy Matters"}

[Why Structure Matters]{.slide-title}

![Artwork by Allison Horst](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/tidy_data.png){width="75%" fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#tidy-explained data-menu-title="Tidy Explained"}

[Tidy Data Makes Analysis Possible]{.slide-title}

![Artwork by Allison Horst](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/tidy_data.png){width="55%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**With tidy data:**
- Functions work as expected
- Grouping operations are straightforward
- Visualization is simple
- Analysis code is readable

**Tidy data isn't a tool—it's a way of thinking**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#three-principles data-menu-title="Three Principles"}

[The Three Principles of Tidy Data]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**1. Every column is a variable**
- One type of information per column
- Example: `height`, `species`, `site_id`

**2. Every row is an observation**  
- One individual/unit per row
- Example: One plant, one measurement event

**3. Every cell is a single value**
- No merged cells
- No lists within cells
- No "see notes" references
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#building-blocks data-menu-title="Building Blocks"}

[Building Blocks: Definitions]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Variable:** A characteristic being measured, counted, or described
- Examples: `temperature`, `species_code`, `plot_number`

**Observation:** A single "data point" for which variables are recorded
- Example: One plant at one time

**Value:** The specific measurement, count, or description
- Example: `3.2`, `"ACRU"`, `42`

**Entity:** Each type of observation  
- Example: If measuring plants AND sites, you have two entities
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#tidy-example data-menu-title="Tidy Example"}

[Example: Tidy Data]{.slide-title}

::: code-text
```
id    date        site   species  height_cm
1     2024-01-15  A      ACRU     120
2     2024-01-15  A      PIST     85
3     2024-01-16  B      ACRU     142
4     2024-01-16  B      QURU     98
```
:::

::: body-text
✅ Each column = one variable  
✅ Each row = one plant observation  
✅ Each cell = one value

**This structure makes analysis straightforward**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#variable-principle data-menu-title="Variable Principle"}

[Principle 1: Each Column is a Variable]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/tidy_variables.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Test:** Look down a column. Is it all the same TYPE of information?

**Good:** All dates, all species codes, all heights  
**Bad:** Mix of dates and temperatures in one column
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#observation-principle data-menu-title="Observation Principle"}

[Principle 2: Each Row is an Observation]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/tidy_observations.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Test:** Look across a row. Does it describe ONE thing?

**Good:** All measurements from one plant at one time  
**Bad:** Measurements from multiple plants in one row
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#value-principle data-menu-title="Value Principle"}

[Principle 3: Each Cell is a Single Value]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/tidy_values.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Test:** Look at each cell. Is it atomic?

**Good:** `42`, `"oak"`, `2024-01-15`  
**Bad:** `"42, 38, 45"`, `"oak/maple"`, `"see notes"`
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#untidy-intro data-menu-title="Untidy Introduction"}

[Recognizing Untidy Data]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Anything that violates the three principles is untidy**

Common violations:
1. Multiple tables in one spreadsheet
2. Column headers are data values
3. Multiple observations per row
4. Variables stored in rows
5. Same observation across multiple rows
6. Multiple types of observational units in same table

**Most real-world data is untidy when you first get it**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#multiple-tables data-menu-title="Multiple Tables"}

[Untidy: Multiple Tables]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/excel-org-01.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Three separate tables embedded in one sheet

**Why it's untidy:** Which rows belong to which table?

**How to fix:** Separate into three distinct files or sheets
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#inconsistent-columns data-menu-title="Inconsistent Columns"}

[Untidy: Inconsistent Columns]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/excel-org-04.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Looking down a column reveals different types of information

**Why it's untidy:** Violates "each column is ONE variable"

**Test:** What units does this column have? If you can't answer, it's untidy
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#inconsistent-rows data-menu-title="Inconsistent Rows"}

[Untidy: Inconsistent Rows]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/excel-org-03.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Looking across a row reveals multiple observations

**Why it's untidy:** Violates "each row is ONE observation"

**Red flag:** Needing to skip rows when reading data
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#marginal-stats data-menu-title="Marginal Stats"}

[Untidy: Marginal Sums and Statistics]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/excel-org-05.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Totals, means, or summaries in the table

**Why it's untidy:**  
- Violates "each column is a variable" (summary ≠ same variable)
- Violates "each row is an observation" (summary ≠ single observation)

**Solution:** Calculate summaries in code, not in data
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#wide-format data-menu-title="Wide Format"}

[Untidy: Wide Format (Multiple Observations per Row)]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/untidy_1.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Two plants per row (`sp1code`, `sp2code`, `sp1height`, `sp2height`)

**Why it's untidy:** Each row contains TWO observations (two plants)

**Consequence:** Adding a third species requires new columns
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#wide-to-long data-menu-title="Wide to Long"}

[From Wide to Long]{.slide-title}

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Wide (untidy):**
```
site  sp1   sp2   height1  height2
A     ACRU  PIST  120      85
```

Multiple observations per row
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Long (tidy):**
```
site  species  height
A     ACRU     120
A     PIST     85
```

One observation per row
:::
:::

::: body-text
**This transformation enables analysis**

We'll learn how to do this in R next week
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#why-tidy data-menu-title="Why Tidy"}

[Why Tidy Data Matters]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Efficiency:**  
- Same tools work on different datasets
- Less reinventing the wheel

**Collaboration:**  
- Others can use same workflows
- Shared vocabulary

**Reuse:**  
- Techniques transfer across projects
- Build on previous work

**Generalizability:**  
- Tools built for one dataset work on others
- R's vectorized operations shine with tidy data
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#normalization data-menu-title="Normalization"}

[Data Normalization]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Normalization** = Removing redundancy to simplify analysis

**In normalized data:**
- Separate tables for each entity type
- Observations (rows) are unique
- Each column is either identifying or measured
- Each table follows tidy principles

**Example:** Plant measurements and site information in separate tables
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#denormalized data-menu-title="Denormalized"}

[Denormalized Data]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/denormalized.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Problem:** Site information (`name`, `altitude`) repeated in every row

**Red flag:** Same values appearing multiple times

**Why it's problematic:**  
- Wastes space
- Increases error risk (typos in repeated data)
- Update anomalies (change site name in one place but not others)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#normalized data-menu-title="Normalized"}

[Normalized Data]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/normalized.png){width="75%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Solution:** Two tables
- **Plants table:** Plant observations
- **Sites table:** Site information

**Connect them using:** Site ID (a **key**)

**Next lecture:** How to reconnect these tables when needed
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#two-entities data-menu-title="Two Entities"}

[Why Two Tables?]{.slide-title}

![](../../images/lecture_tidy_data/two_entities.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Recognize two entities:**
1. Plants (species, height measurements)
2. Sites (location, altitude, site name)

**Each entity gets its own table**

**Different entities ≠ different tables**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#uncomfortable data-menu-title="Uncomfortable"}

[This Might Feel Uncomfortable]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Common reaction:** "But I need site AND plant data together for analysis!"

**You're right!** You will need them together

**Solution:** We'll learn **joins** (Week 7)

**For now:** Focus on recognizing whether data is normalized

**Trust the process:** Normalized data + joins = powerful, flexible analysis
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#thinking-exercise data-menu-title="Thinking Exercise"}

[Thinking Exercise]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Imagine you're studying:**
- Birds observed at different sites
- Each site has habitat characteristics
- Multiple observations per site across dates

**Question:** How many entities do you have?

**Pause and think before advancing**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#thinking-answer data-menu-title="Thinking Answer"}

[Thinking Exercise: Answer]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Three entities:**

1. **Bird observations** (species, count, date)
2. **Sites** (location, habitat type, area)
3. **Survey events** (date, time, observer)

**That means:** Three tables

**Connected by:** Site ID and survey ID (keys)

**This is relational data modeling** (next lecture)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#best-practices data-menu-title="Best Practices"}

[Tidy Data Best Practices Summary]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**The Three Principles:**
1. Every column is a variable
2. Every row is an observation  
3. Every cell is a single value

**Additional guidelines:**
- Design tables to add rows, not columns
- Use descriptive column names (no spaces!)
- Include a header row
- No merged cells
- No color-coding as data

**Remember:** Tidy ≠ normalized (both are important!)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#diagnosis data-menu-title="Diagnosis"}

[Diagnosing Untidy Data]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Before writing ANY code, ask:**

1. What are the variables? (List them)
2. What are the observations? (What's one row?)
3. Are there multiple tables hidden here?
4. Are there multiple entities mixed together?
5. Is anything repeated unnecessarily?

**Once you can answer these, you know what needs fixing**

**Next week:** How to actually FIX untidy data using R
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#real-world data-menu-title="Real World"}

[Real-World Data Is Usually Untidy]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Don't be discouraged!**

Most data you encounter will violate these principles

**Why?**
- Designed for human readability, not analysis
- Created in Excel for manual inspection
- Collected without analysis plan

**Your job:** Recognize the issues and know how to fix them

**Tools we'll use:** `tidyr` and `dplyr` (next week)
:::
